# dsh-carbon
Track the estimated carbon footprint of your DeepSeek Harness sessions, in the terminal and in the w
he estimated carbon footprint of your DeepSeek Harness sessions, in the terminal and in the web GUI.
It takes the idea behind claude-carbon, a local estimate built from token counts with a sourced meth
odology, and applies it to DeepSeek. The numbers are not ported. The published evidence for DeepSeek
is much thinner, and borrowing Anthropic's factors would have produced a confident figure with noth
er, and borrowing Anthropic's factors would have produced a confident figure with nothing behind it.
[代码示例省略，未执行]
## The web GUI
The plugin adds a Carbon row to the sidebar and opens a page in the main panel.
The page leads with a whale, and its colour is the reading: the same green to yellow to red ramp as
the hero, on the same log scale, green up to 250 g and red from 5 kg. It blinks, and beats its fluke
faster as the figure climbs. One character map in `lib/core/whale.mjs` draws it for the page and fo
r the exported card, so the whale on your card is the one you saw on screen.
Under it the estimate is never shown alone. There is a low/high band beside it and a marker showing
where the point estimate sits inside that band. Below that, a row of stripes: one per day, week or m
onth, coloured against the median period rather than a maximum, so a quiet week still reads as a str
ipe next to a busy one. Hovering or tabbing to a stripe names its date, total and session count. The
toolbar switches the window between 7 days, 30, 90, 12 months and all time, remembered per browser,
and shows the change against the previous window of the same length whenever there is one to compar
nd shows the change against the previous window of the same length whenever there is one to compare.
Then two bars split the same four kinds of token twice: how many there were, and what they cost in g
rams. Almost every token in a session is a cache read, and cache reads come to roughly a tenth of th
e grams. Output is half a percent of the tokens and nine tenths of the footprint. One bar would have
ut is half a percent of the tokens and nine tenths of the footprint. One bar would have hidden that.
The rest is smaller. Equivalents in km driven, kettle boils and phone charges, from the same world-a
verage factors the CLI uses. A switch between DeepSeek's own fleet and Azure that applies to every n
umber on the page, totals, sessions, models, stripes and equivalents alike, and is remembered per br
owser. A Method tab with the formula, the deployment assumptions, each factor row with its tier, ban
d, caveat and source, and the cross-checks underneath. English and Chinese, following the host local
e, laid out for narrow main columns.
The page refreshes every 30 seconds while it is visible, when the window regains focus, and on deman
d. The refresh button skips the host's 5-second cache.

## Install
Requirements: DeepSeek Harness **0.2.1-rc.3 or newer** (declared in `dsh.engines.dsh`), and Node **2
2.15+** only if you want the standalone CLI. The plugin itself runs inside the app.
**As a plugin.** The GUI is this half; the CLI comes with it.

### Why R1's factor is worse than V3's
Fitting `energy = a*input + b*output` to the three published R1 points gives a 30% mean error, again
st 2.0% for V3. The reason is diagnostic rather than cosmetic: R1 costs ~19 Wh even for a 100/300-to
ken prompt. Most of its energy is **fixed per query** (long reasoning traces, prefill, scheduling) r
ather than proportional to tokens. A token-only model therefore under-reports short R1 sessions and
over-reports long ones.
`dsh-carbon` reports that error instead of hiding it. A per-query intercept term would fit better, b
ut it needs a count of requests that the log does not cleanly provide, so the limitation is document
ed rather than papered over.
### Why the input factor is the weak one
The three published points are close to collinear, so the input and output terms trade off almost fr
eely. Unconstrained least squares puts the input coefficient **slightly negative** for the DeepSeek
rows, which is obviously wrong and a sign that the data cannot separate prefill from decode. The der
ivation script therefore uses non-negative least squares and carries the input term across from the
Azure fit, where it is positive and identifiable, rescaled to the China grid. It is a borrowed numbe
r, labelled as such.
## How it works
[代码示例省略，未执行]
Cache reads are a prefill residual at 8% of the input factor. DeepSeek's 0.02 cache-hit *price* rati
o is not an energy ratio and is deliberately not used.
Token counts come from the session logs under `~/.dsh/sessions/*/*/session.v4.jsonl.zstd`, reading `
data.usage` on `assistant/message` events and attributing each message to `data.message.source.model
`, so a mid-session model switch is priced correctly. `inputTokens` already excludes cached tokens.
`sync` folds those logs into the store (see The store), and every reading is priced from the store r
ather than the logs, so a pruned transcript no longer loses its footprint.
Assistant messages are deduplicated by `message.id`. A resumed or compacted session can replay messa
ges that are already in the log, and counting a replay twice inflates the token sum with no symptom
other than a larger footprint. `claude-carbon` found roughly 3x inflation from this. Across the logs
read here no session had a repeat, so the count of ignored replays is reported rather than quietly
e no session had a repeat, so the count of ignored replays is reported rather than quietly absorbed.
One implementation detail is worth knowing. The harness *appends* to these logs, one zstd frame per
flush, and a live log had 168 frames. Node's `zstdDecompressSync` decodes only the first frame and s
ilently returns a truncated log. This walks every frame, validating each candidate boundary by attem
pting the decode, and drops a half-written trailing frame, which Node decodes to a partial line rath
er than throwing. Without that, history would be silently under-reported by an order of magnitude.
